result:
At 4:17 in the morning, the city briefly forgets what it is.

The traffic lights continue changing for no one. Storefronts hold their dark reflections. Somewhere, a refrigerator hums behind a wall, keeping faith with the milk. A fox slips between two buildings and pauses beneath a fire escape, its eyes bright with the private knowledge of the night.

In an apartment three floors up, someone wakes from a dream about an ocean.

They do not remember the dream itself—only the color of the water, a blue so deep it seemed to contain weather from other worlds. They sit by the window and watch rain gather on the glass. Each drop catches the amber streetlight, becoming, for one second, a small moving star.

There are moments when the future feels less like a road and more like a room we are already standing in, though the lights are off.

The person at the window thinks of all the lives they might have lived: the one in which they stayed, the one in which they left, the one in which they learned to play the piano, the one in which they called their mother back. These lives do not accuse them. They simply drift nearby, translucent as breath.

Then, from somewhere below, a laugh rises into the rain.

It is sudden and imperfect. It belongs to two strangers sharing an umbrella, or perhaps to a delivery driver who has remembered something funny. The sound travels upward, finds the open window, and enters the room.

The person smiles.

Morning is still a long way off, but the world has begun returning to itself. The city remembers its name. Pipes knock in the walls. A bus groans awake. In a kitchen across the street, someone turns on a light.

And for now, that is enough.

A light.  
A window.  
The blue memory of an ocean.

The quiet, stubborn fact that the day will come.
